query: For nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution, what governs whether structural and chemical stability is maintained across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled comparison, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, define the conditions under which the prediction should hold, identify supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: For equimolar multi‐metal nanoparticles, stability over catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges (473–1923 K) is determined by the balance between entropy‐driven lattice stabilization (which produces significant lattice distortions and short‐range ordering that slow atomic diffusion) and thermally activated atomic diffusion that can trigger phase separation. In other words, if the entropic stabilization (manifested via high configurational entropy and associated diffusion barriers) remains dominant relative to thermal energy, the solid solution is retained; if the operating temperature exceeds a critical threshold enabling rapid diffusion, structural and chemical inhomogeneities (e.g., elemental segregation or secondary phase formation) will emerge.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles comprising five or more metals in near‐equal atomic ratios, crystallized as a single-phase solid solution with high configurational entropy and intrinsic lattice distortions.
generation.intervention: Systematically expose the nanoparticles to a controlled temperature regimen covering the 473–1923 K range (in inert or controlled atmospheres) while monitoring structural and compositional changes.
generation.conditions: Experiments should be performed under controlled atmospheres (to avoid extrinsic oxidation effects) and with well-defined heating rates and dwell times that mimic catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The high configurational entropy that creates lattice distortions and subtle short-range ordering, which in turn imparts high activation barriers to atomic diffusion.
generation.mechanism: Entropy stabilization induces local lattice distortions and short-range ordering, which elevate the diffusion activation energy and slow atomic rearrangements. At lower operating temperatures, thermal energy is insufficient to overcome these barriers, thus maintaining a homogeneous solid solution. At elevated temperatures—if thermal energy exceeds the entropic stabilization energy—the increased atomic mobility results in segregation or phase separation. Thus, the competition between TΔS_mix (stabilizing) and the temperature-driven activation of diffusion (destabilizing) governs the structural and chemical stability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Within a defined temperature window (up to a material-specific critical temperature), the nanoparticles will preserve their single-phase, homogeneous structure. Beyond this threshold, measurable signs of phase decomposition, compositional segregation, or the onset of secondary phase formation will be observed.
generation.baseline: Initial characterization at room temperature and at the lower bound of the operating temperature, showing a uniform single-phase solid solution (verified by XRD, TEM/STEM, and elemental mapping).
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold provided the operating temperature remains below the critical threshold at which the thermal activation energy overcomes the entropic diffusion barriers. This threshold is system dependent and may approach the upper limits of the given 473–1923 K range, especially under prolonged high-temperature exposure.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty in the exact determination of the critical temperature where entropy stabilization no longer prevents diffusion, as well as in the relative contributions of dynamic lattice vibrations versus static lattice distortions. This proposal builds on findings from entropy stabilization and sluggish diffusion (e.g., PMC7069714 evidence) and scaling laws for lattice distortions (e.g., PMC10983832), while extending them to catalytic and thermoelectric regimes.

falsification_experiment.design: Heat a series of the HEA nanoparticles in an inert atmosphere using controlled heating protocols to temperatures at, below, and above the predicted critical threshold. Monitor real-time phase evolution using in-situ high-temperature XRD and follow with TEM/STEM-EDS analyses post-treatment. Perform tests with varying heating rates and exposure durations to assess the balance between entropic stabilization and thermally activated diffusion.
measurements: Phase identification and monitoring by in-situ XRD
Morphology and elemental distribution via TEM/STEM with EDS mapping
Assessment of diffusion kinetics possibly via complementary MD simulations or tracer diffusion measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles either remain phase pure and compositionally homogeneous even beyond the predicted critical temperature, or if phase separation/segregation occurs at temperatures significantly lower than expected, then the hypothesis that entropic stabilization via lattice distortions governs stability is refuted.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractLattice distortions are intrinsic features of all solid solution alloys associated with varying atomic radii; this phenomenon facilitates the formation of single-phase solid solutions. Using high-entropy alloys (HEAs), as an example, we investigate the influence of variations in inter-atomic separations for stabilizing and controlling their structural, mechanical, and thermodynamic properties. This is done through a combination of statistical mechanics analysis and molecular dynamics simulations on simplified 2D systems, as well as a 3D crystals with harmonic and anharmonic inter-atomic bonds with varying natural inter-atomic separations. We demonstrate that the impact of this inter-atomic length disorder (representing static lattice distortion) and temperature fluctuations (representing dynamic lattice distortion) on fundamental and universal thermodynamic, structural, and elastic characteristics are similar and can be unified through effective temperature; i.e. a scaling law for HEAs that establishes a relationship between these factors. The stability of the MEA-NPs is critical for their practical application at elevated temperatures. We, therefore, performed an in situ stability test in the electron microscope from room temperature up to 873 K, annealing the NPs at each test point for at least 30 min. As shown in Fig. 4A, the ultrafine Ru-5 MEA-NPs maintain their uniform dispersion throughout the in situ tests up to 873 K and demonstrate superior size stability after high-temperature annealing. In addition, the NPs are still in a homogeneous alloy structure without elemental segregation or phase separation (Fig. 4B), showing their structural stability. Note that the Co and Ni after annealing are slightly less than the nominal composition, which is likely due to metal evaporation at high temperature in the microscope vacuum. We also confirmed the alloy structure macroscopically by powder and synchrotron x-ray diffraction, showing a single-phase fcc structure with a fitted lattice constant of 3.673 Å (fig. S3, B and C).
